title: Ethics and Living Together
description: Ten calm, balanced essays on living with others: the duty to vote, tipping, sharing the road with cyclists, changed promises, a shared garden, honest recommendation letters, noise through the wall, arguing with someone you love, the ethics of cosplay and visiting a grieving family.

lessons.title: Must We Vote?
lessons.summary: An essay weighs voting as a duty against voting as a right and settles on a modest civic habit.
lessons.text:
Every election season, a familiar argument returns to kitchen tables. Is voting a duty that each citizen owes the community, or a right that each of us may use or leave alone? Both answers deserve a patient hearing.

Those who call voting a duty begin with a simple observation. A democracy works only if many people take part. When turnout falls, decisions are made by a smaller and less representative group. Some countries take this view so seriously that their laws expressly require citizens to vote. In Australia, the law expressly requires every adult citizen to vote, although, since the ballot is secret, nobody can check what a voter writes on it.

The other side is no less serious. A right, they argue, includes the right not to use it. A citizen who finds no candidate convincing may feel that staying home is the honest choice. Others feel a deep distrust of politics itself, and their distrust is often not laziness at all but a judgment formed by years of broken promises.

There is also the problem of too much information. Modern voters face a flood of slogans and contradictory figures, and some of them fall into a kind of paralysis. Faced with contradictory evidence, a careful citizen may conclude that any choice would be a guess, and the paralysis ends, quietly, at home.

How, then, should we decide? A useful criterion may be this: not whether my single vote will change the result, which it almost never does, but whether I have done my share in a common project. By that criterion, voting looks less like a heroic act and more like paying one's part of a shared bill.

It also helps to look past the theater of campaigns. A charismatic speaker can stir a crowd, and a visionary plan can promise a new age, but charm is not a program, and the most visionary speeches are often the least specific. Motivational slogans tell us how a candidate wishes us to feel, not what he or she will do; no motivational poster has ever written a budget. Sometimes the underdog, the less charismatic candidate with modest promises, has thought harder about the actual work. Yet rooting for the underdog is no better a criterion than charm. What matters is the record and the plan.

So where does this leave a citizen standing at the crossroads, unsure whether to go or to stay? Voting is not a sacred command, and a person who stays home after real thought has committed no crime. But the habit is worth keeping, because a democracy is built from small, repeated acts. Even at a crossroads where every road looks poor, choosing the least poor of them is a quiet way of saying: this country is partly mine.

Questions:
Why do some people say that voting is a duty?
A democracy works only if many people take part, and low turnout leaves decisions to a smaller group.
What does the law in Australia expressly require?
It expressly requires every adult citizen to vote.
How can contradictory information lead to paralysis?
A voter faced with it may feel that any choice would be a guess, and so the voter stays home.
What criterion does the writer suggest?
The writer suggests asking whether one has done one's share in a common project.
Why should voters look past charismatic speakers?
Charm is not a program; what matters is the record and the plan.

lessons.title: What We Owe the Waitress
lessons.summary: A column on tipping sets the case for tips beside the case against them and reaches a practical answer.
lessons.text:
In a small diner off the highway, a waitress refills your coffee without being asked. The free refill is a cherished custom in the United States, and so is what comes next: at the end of the meal, you leave a tip of fifteen or twenty percent. Visitors often find the custom puzzling, and so, if they are honest, do many locals.

The case for tipping is chiefly a case about wages. In many states, restaurant workers may be paid a low base wage on the understanding that tips will make up the rest. The waitress who brought your refill and poured extra gravy over your potatoes is not being rewarded for her smile; she is being paid for her work. The customer who walks out without tipping has left as a debtor, a person who owes money and has chosen not to pay it. No court will pursue the debt, but he remains a debtor all the same.

Critics of tipping do not dispute that the worker deserves the money. Their objection is chiefly to the method. A tip makes a worker's income depend on the mood, the generosity and sometimes the prejudices of strangers. Pay that rises and falls with such things, the critics argue, is incompatible with the idea of a fair wage. Researchers have long reported that tips vary widely for the same service, for reasons that have little to do with the quality of the work.

Some restaurants have tried another way. They put the service charge upfront, printed clearly on the menu, and pay their staff a full wage from it. Prices look higher, but the arrangement is honest and upfront. A friend of mine runs a small consultancy that advises restaurant owners, and her consultancy has helped several of them make this change. Other owners have found a loophole: a small "kitchen fee" in fine print, which customers rarely notice and which the owners keep. The loophole gives a restaurant the look of fairness without the substance.

Each position contains something admirable. The wish to reward good work is admirable, and so is the demand that a living wage should not depend on luck. The two views are not truly incompatible; they belong to different stages of the same reform.

What, then, should an ordinary diner do tonight? We may argue for better laws, but the waitress in front of us lives inside the system as it is. My uncle, who dislikes tipping on principle, tips twenty percent anyhow. "My argument is with the system," he says, "not with her." The gravy may have been cold, but she brought it anyhow.

Questions:
Why is the case for tipping chiefly a case about wages?
In many states, restaurant workers are paid a low base wage, and tips make up the rest.
In what sense does a customer who leaves no tip become a debtor?
He owes the worker money for her work and does not pay it.
Why do critics say that tipping is incompatible with a fair wage?
A tip makes a worker's income depend on the mood and the prejudices of strangers.
How is an upfront service charge different from the loophole?
An upfront charge is printed clearly and pays a full wage; the loophole is a hidden fee that the owners keep.
Why does the writer's uncle tip anyhow?
He believes that his argument is with the system, not with the waitress.

lessons.title: Sharing the Road
lessons.summary: A week of cycling beside a loch in Scotland helps a writer weigh the complaints of drivers and cyclists.
lessons.text:
Some years ago I spent a week cycling around a loch in the Highlands of Scotland. The road followed the water for forty miles, narrow and winding, with stone walls on one side and the cold, bright loch on the other. I rode a sturdy old bicycle, and for the first time I understood, from the saddle, a question I had only ever considered from behind a steering wheel: how should drivers and cyclists share a road?

The driver's complaint is familiar. A cyclist on a narrow road can impede traffic for miles. Cars gather behind him, and sooner or later someone overtakes on a blind bend. Some cyclists, drivers add, ignore red lights as if the rules were written for others.

The cyclist's reply is equally familiar, and on that loch road I learned its force. Sturdy as my bicycle was, a single gust of air from a passing truck could push it sideways, and the gusts off the water were worse. Twice I felt my front wheel skid on wet leaves at the roadside, which is exactly where cyclists are expected to ride. A skid at speed could have been serious. I finished each day with shaky hands, not from effort but from attention, and with a shaky faith in strangers.

The gravest cases reach a coroner. When a coroner examines a serious accident involving a bicycle, the conclusion is often the same sad sentence: the driver did not see the cyclist in time. The causes are usually small and careless, which is why they can be avoided.

Both sides, then, have a point, and the useful question is what each can do. For the cyclist, the duties are modest: obey the signals, use bright lights in the evening, and pull in at the roadside when a line of cars has formed, so as not to impede others for long. For the driver, the duty is mostly patience: waiting rather than passing on a bend, leaving a wide gap, and dipping the headlights at night. A cyclist caught in full headlights on a dark road cannot see the edge of the road at all.

The greatest hurdle is not the law but imagination. Many drivers have never ridden a bicycle in heavy traffic, and many cyclists forget how small and sudden they appear from a car. Each side sees the other as a hurdle in its path, rather than as a person trying to get home.

On my last evening I stopped at the roadside to watch the light fade over the loch. A van slowed behind me, waited, and passed with a wide, careful gap. The driver raised one hand from the wheel. It was a small gesture, but it contained the whole argument: the road is shared, and sharing it costs each of us only a little patience.

Questions:
Where did the writer spend a week cycling?
The writer cycled around a loch in Scotland.
What do drivers complain about?
A cyclist can impede traffic for miles, and some cyclists ignore red lights.
Why did the writer finish each day with shaky hands?
Gusts pushed the bicycle sideways, and wet leaves made the wheel skid.
What does a coroner often conclude about such accidents?
The coroner often concludes that the driver did not see the cyclist in time.
What does the writer see as the greatest hurdle?
The greatest hurdle is imagination, because each side forgets how the road looks to the other.

lessons.title: A Promise in Changing Weather
lessons.summary: A writer must change a promise to a friend and weighs the strict and the flexible views of promising.
lessons.text:
Last spring I promised my friend Tom that I would help him move on the first weekend of June. Then, at the eleventh hour, I was offered an interview for a job I had wanted for years, on that very Saturday. I did not relish the call I would have to make. It raised a question as old as moral philosophy: does a promise bind us whatever happens, or does it assume that the world will stay roughly as it was?

The strict view is old and serious. A promise is valuable precisely because it does not bend. If promises could be dropped whenever something better came along, they would evaporate the moment they became a burden. One eighteenth-century treatise on morals put the point with force: a person who makes a promise has given away a small part of his freedom and cannot take it back merely because he regrets the bargain. Readers in the eighteenth century found that treatise severe, and many still do, but few have found it simply wrong.

The strict view also matches something that seems innate in us. Small children protest when a promise is broken: "But you said!" A sense of fairness appears very early in life, which suggests that our respect for promises may be partly innate rather than merely taught.

Yet history shows a more flexible practice. In medieval London, a mercer, a merchant who dealt in fine cloth, might seal a sale by shaking hands, and a mercer who broke his word could lose his place in the trade. But the merchants' customs allowed for storms at sea and ships that never arrived. A promise, they understood, rests on ordinary expectations. When those change completely, the promise is not so much broken as overtaken. Many promises carry a silent expiration date: not a date on the calendar, but the point at which the conditions they assumed no longer hold.

The difficulty is that a person who wishes to escape a promise is always tempted to announce its expiration. The interview felt to me like a storm at sea; to Tom, it might look like a better offer. Who decides?

In the end I called Tom at once, rather than at the eleventh hour, and asked him rather than told him. I offered to come on Friday evening and to pay for movers on Saturday. Tom, who had not relished the idea of carrying a piano without me, laughed and said that the interview mattered more than the piano. Our concord survived, I think, because I treated the promise as his as much as mine. When circumstances change, the honest course is to return to the person who holds the other half of a promise and agree on new terms.

Promises do bend, then, but they should not evaporate in silence. They bend best when we bend them together, early, and in concord.

Questions:
What did the writer promise Tom?
The writer promised to help Tom move on the first weekend of June.
What did the eighteenth-century treatise argue?
It argued that a person who makes a promise gives away part of his freedom and cannot take it back merely out of regret.
What did a medieval mercer understand about promises?
He understood that a promise rests on ordinary expectations, which a storm at sea can change.
How did the writer keep the concord with Tom?
The writer called early, asked rather than told, and offered other help.

lessons.title: The Basil Problem
lessons.summary: A community garden runs into the tragedy of the commons and solves it with simple local rules.
lessons.text:
Our community garden sits on an empty lot between two apartment buildings. Each member has a small private bed, and in the middle there is a shared bed of herbs, a shared shed of tools and one long, shared hose. For years the arrangement worked well. Then, one summer, the shared bed began to look tired, the tools began to rust and the hose split. Nobody had done anything terrible. That was precisely the problem.

Ruth, a retired mathematician whose bed is next to mine, explained it to me with a pencil. As a mathematician, she had spent thirty years building models of terrestrial ecosystems, the forests and fields of dry land. On the back of a seed packet she began to doodle a line that rose quickly and then leveled off. "This is a logistic curve," she said. "It describes growth that slows as it approaches a limit. Our basil grows like this." Then she added a second doodle, a straight line rising across the first. "And this is how much basil we take." Where the two lines crossed, the basil began to die. Ruth had found logistic curves everywhere in her terrestrial models, from forests to fields; now she saw one in our herbs.

What she was describing is often called the tragedy of the commons. When a resource is shared and free, each user gains the whole benefit of taking a little more, while the cost is spread across everyone. Nobody in our garden was a burglar; nobody came at night with a bag. We simply smuggled home a little more than our share. A burglar at least knows that he is stealing. Those of us who smuggled basil did not even notice.

The tools told the same story. Shears left wet in the shed developed a fine coat of corrosion, because oiling them was everyone's job and therefore no one's. When the shed door jammed, someone forced it open by brute force and broke the hinge. After the hose split, members carried water in buckets, and one of them strained a tendon in her wrist. The tendon healed in a month. The garden took longer.

The bees behaved better than we did. They carried pollen from bed to bed without asking whose flowers were whose, and that pollen helped everyone's tomatoes. They took what they needed and paid in work.

The solution was not brute force either. The economist Elinor Ostrom, who won a Nobel Prize for studying how communities manage shared resources, found that successful commons usually have clear local rules made by the users themselves. We set a weekly limit on herbs, made a schedule for oiling the tools and put a notebook in the shed. Within a season, the basil had recovered and the corrosion was gone.

Questions:
What did Ruth doodle on the back of a seed packet?
She doodled a logistic curve, a line that rises quickly and then levels off.
Why does the writer say that nobody was a burglar?
Each member simply smuggled home a little more than a fair share.
What happened to the shared tools?
The shears developed corrosion, and the shed door was forced open by brute force.
How did the bees behave differently from the gardeners?
They carried pollen to everyone's plants and took only what they needed.
How did the garden solve its problem?
The members made clear local rules, such as a weekly limit on herbs.

lessons.title: The Honest Letter
lessons.summary: A high school teacher writes a recommendation letter that is warm, specific and true.
lessons.text:
Every fall, a small pile of requests appears on my desk. I teach biology at a public high school, and my students ask me for letters of recommendation for college. It is one of the pleasures of the job and one of its quiet moral tests: how honest should a recommendation be?

The pressure to exaggerate is enormous. Admissions officers read thousands of letters, and in many of them every student is "the best I have taught in twenty years." Such phrases once excited readers; now they excite no one, because everyone uses them. If every other letter shouts, a calm one may sound like a warning.

This year the pile included a request from Daniel, a thoughtful, slightly awkward boy whose yearbook photo shows him holding a plastic model of the human brain. His fascination with the brain began when his grandmother had a stroke and he wanted to understand why she could still sing but could no longer speak. He is applying to study neuroscience at several universities, including my own alma mater. His fascination is real; his grades are good but not brilliant; his lab reports are careful but often late.

I could have written that Daniel was a genius. I am a sincere admirer of the boy, but an admirer is not the same as a witness, and a letter of recommendation is a kind of testimony. If I exaggerate, I spend my own credibility, and next year, when a truly exceptional student asks me for a letter, the readers at my alma mater may discount every word.

Yet honesty can also wound. A colleague of mine once described a student, in a letter, as "adequate." It was true, and it was devastating. A word like that, sent where the student can never answer it, is not slander, since it is not false, but it can do the work of slander.

So I tried to write what I knew. I described the yearbook photo, his fascination with how a damaged brain recovers, and his patience with the microscope. I admitted, in one sentence, that he sometimes misses deadlines, and added that he always finishes the work. I left out the trivia that fills too many letters, such as his record in the school trivia contest, and kept to what would matter in a neuroscience lab.

Before sending it, I read the letter aloud and found two typos. A typo is a small thing, but it suggests hurry, and hurry suggests that the writer did not care. I corrected both typos and sent the letter well before the winter break.

Daniel will hear from the universities before commencement in June. Whatever they decide, I will sit at his commencement with a clear conscience. In a pile of shouting letters, a calm and specific one is easier to believe, and it may even excite a reader who has grown tired of praise.

Questions:
Why do strong phrases no longer excite readers?
Everyone uses them, so they have lost their force.
What began Daniel's fascination with the brain?
His grandmother had a stroke, and he wanted to understand why she could sing but not speak.
Why does the teacher say that an admirer is not the same as a witness?
A letter of recommendation is a kind of testimony.
How can a true word do the work of slander?
A word like "adequate" can do great harm even though it is not false.

lessons.title: Through the Wall
lessons.summary: An apartment dweller thinks fairly about noise, and a power outage helps a building agree on rules.
lessons.text:
I live on the third floor of an old brick building with thin walls. Above me lives Marcus, a music student who practices the saxophone every evening from six to eight. Below me, four retired women play mahjong two afternoons a week, and the click of the tiles rises through the floor like light rain. Next door, on weekends, a young couple plays techno, a steady electronic beat that I feel in the wall more than I hear it.

My aim is to think fairly about a problem that every shared building faces: whose noise is acceptable, and when?

The first thing to admit is that I am noisy too. My washer shakes the kitchen floor during its spin cycle, and my old air conditioner rattles all summer. When I fill the bathtub late at night, the pipes groan through three apartments, and when the bathtub drains, they groan again. The building makes noise by itself as well: the compressor on the roof hums day and night. Even the internet once made noise. The oldest tenant still remembers the whistle of a dial-up modem crossing the hallway at midnight. Today the modem only blinks.

Last year, a woman on the fifth floor lost patience with a couple who played techno until two in the morning. She wrote to the landlord, who threatened them with eviction. The threat solved the problem and created a worse one. The couple moved out, and the building lost two tenants who had been friendly in every other way. An eviction is a powerful tool, but a blunt one, and it should be the last step, not the first.

Then came the summer outage. A storm cut the power for a whole night. The compressor stopped, the air conditioner stopped, the washer stopped, and the building fell into a silence I had never heard. People came out onto the stairs with candles, and the mahjong players brought cold tea. Marcus played the saxophone softly on the landing, and nobody asked him to stop. During the outage I learned the names of people I had passed in the hall for a decade.

What did the outage teach? Chiefly that noise is easier to bear from someone we know. A sound from a stranger feels like an intrusion; the same sound from a person with a name feels like life. Most quarrels about noise could be settled by a knock on the door and a friendly conversation before anyone writes to a landlord.

Our building now has a few modest rules, agreed on in the lobby rather than handed down. Music stops at ten during the week, nobody runs a washer after eleven, and anyone planning a party slips a note under the nearby doors. The walls are as thin as ever, but the building feels quieter, because we have stopped treating every sound as an insult.

Questions:
What sounds reach the writer through the walls and the floor?
The writer hears the saxophone from above, the mahjong tiles from below and techno from next door.
Why does the writer admit to being noisy too?
The washer shakes the floor, the air conditioner rattles, and the bathtub makes the pipes groan.
Why does the writer think the eviction was a mistake?
It cost the building two friendly tenants; an eviction should be the last step, not the first.
What happened during the outage?
The building fell silent, and people gathered on the stairs.

lessons.title: Arguing with My Father
lessons.summary: A daughter and her father, who disagree about the news, learn a few rules for arguing with love.
lessons.text:
My father and I disagree about almost everything that appears in the news. I am his only daughter, and for years our arguments followed the same sad pattern. One of us would make a remark at dinner, the other would answer sharply, and within ten minutes my father would go ballistic, his voice rising until my mother left the room. I would respond with cold defiance, folding my arms and refusing to admit even the points I privately agreed with.

We loved each other, and our love was unconditional; neither of us ever doubted it. But unconditional love, I slowly learned, does not mean unconditional agreement, and it does not by itself teach people how to argue.

What changed things was partly a popular book about the brain. When we feel attacked, it explained, the heart beats faster, and the frontal lobes, the part of the brain behind the forehead that helps us plan and hold back our impulses, have a harder time doing their work. In the heat of an argument, in other words, we are less able to think. No wonder my father went ballistic over a tax policy he could explain calmly the next morning.

Knowing this, my father and I made a few rules. The first was to stop when either of us felt our heart racing and to return to the subject an hour later, when our frontal lobes had come back to work. The second was to stop collecting ammo. Each of us had been storing old remarks, the way a soldier stores ammo for the next battle: something said at a wedding years before, something written in a birthday card. We agreed to argue about one thing at a time and to leave the old ammo in the past.

The third rule was about words. My father used to call my views hysterical, and I used to say that only a weirdo would believe everything he heard on the radio. Neither remark was an argument. To call someone hysterical is to dismiss a feeling instead of answering a reason; to call someone a weirdo is to say that he is not worth answering at all. We agreed to describe the idea, never the person.

The fourth rule was the hardest: no victory laps. When one of us made a good point, the other was allowed to admit it without the winner getting up to strut around the kitchen. My father, I confess, used to strut a little, and I used to meet his good points with defiance rather than thanks.

We still disagree, but our arguments now end with both of us at the table. The aim of arguing with someone you love, I have come to think, is not to win, but to understand why a person you respect sees the world differently. The love was always unconditional. The patience we had to learn.

Questions:
What used to happen when the writer and her father argued?
Her father would go ballistic, and she would respond with cold defiance.
Why are people less able to think in the heat of an argument?
The frontal lobes, which help us plan and hold back our impulses, have a harder time doing their work.
What does the writer mean by collecting ammo?
She means storing old remarks to use in the next argument.
Why did they stop using words such as "hysterical" and "weirdo"?
Such words dismiss a person instead of answering an idea.

lessons.title: Borrowed Faces
lessons.summary: A parent at a fan convention thinks about what cosplay fans owe the creators and makers they borrow from.
lessons.text:
Every summer, a convention center near my city fills with goblins, wizards and at least one giant squid. The convention is devoted to comics, films and games, and its most visible pleasure is cosplay, the art of making and wearing costumes of fictional characters. My daughter, who is nine, went as a snowflake last year, in a white dress covered with paper crystals she had cut herself. I went as the giant squid, mainly because she asked me to.

Cosplay is cheerful, but it raises a few honest questions, which fans of cosplay argue about with surprising seriousness. Is it right to dress as a character someone else created? May a fan sell costumes based on a studio's designs? And what does one fan owe another whose original costume he admires and copies?

The first question is the easiest. Fans have always borrowed from the stories they love, and most creators welcome it. A crowd of children dressed as a cartoon villain's little minions is the best advertisement a studio could wish for. Wearing a costume is a form of praise, and no one thinks a boy dressed as a minion has stolen anything.

The second question is harder. Selling a few handmade costumes at a convention is generally tolerated, but copying a studio's designs on a large scale and selling them online is another matter. The line falls roughly where admiration becomes business: wearing a goblin mask is a tribute, while producing a thousand goblin masks for sale is a commercial decision in which the creator has a right to share.

The third question is the one fans discuss most. Many costumes are invented by fans who interpret a character in their own way. Last year I saw a remarkable goblin whose design came from an eighteenth-century engraving in a book of fairy tales. Its maker had studied the engraving for weeks. She had matched its wild hair with dyed cony, an old word for rabbit fur, and the cony stood up around the face like dry grass. She carried a belt of small glass bottles, each labeled as a different potion: a sleep potion, a courage potion, a potion against bad weather. It was the most adventurous costume in the hall.

Within a month, copies of that goblin appeared online, sold by people who never mentioned its maker. Among fans of cosplay, that is the real offense. Copying an adventurous idea is natural; failing to credit it is not. The rule is simple: if you build on someone's design, name them. For many makers, recognition is the holy grail of the hobby, and that grail costs nothing to give.

My daughter has already learned the rule. When a girl at the convention admired her snowflake dress, she explained proudly that she had copied the crystals from a library book about snowflakes, and she showed the girl the page.

Questions:
What is cosplay?
Cosplay is the art of making and wearing costumes of fictional characters.
Where did the design of the remarkable goblin come from?
It came from an eighteenth-century engraving in a book of fairy tales.
What was the real offense when copies of the goblin appeared online?
The sellers never mentioned the maker of the original design.
What is the holy grail of the hobby for many makers?
For many makers, recognition is the holy grail of the hobby.

lessons.title: Showing Up
lessons.summary: When the street's old midwife dies, a neighbor hesitates, then learns how to visit a family sitting shiva.
lessons.text:
For forty years, Mrs. Levin was the midwife of our street. Before she retired, she had helped deliver half the children on our block, including my own two daughters. When she died this winter, at 91, the whole street felt it. She was dearly loved, and, like many people who are dearly loved, she had never seemed to need anything from anyone.

Her son, David, flew home from London, where he works as a barrister, a lawyer who argues cases in court. The family announced that they would sit shiva at Mrs. Levin's house. I am not Jewish, and I had to ask a friend what that meant. Shiva, she explained, is the traditional period of mourning after a Jewish funeral. For seven days the family stays at home, and friends and members of the community come to visit, bring food and sit with them.

I hesitated for two days. I was afraid of saying something foolish or breaking a custom I did not understand. My hesitation raised a common question for all of us who live side by side: when someone nearby is in mourning, is it kinder to keep a respectful distance or to show up, however awkward we feel?

There is a real case for distance. A house full of visitors can be a burden. Some families want privacy, and respecting that wish is a kind of courtesy.

My friend, however, gave me some simple advice. The point of a shiva visit, she said, is not to say anything clever. Visitors traditionally wait for the family to speak first, and they may sit in silence for a while. You come, you sit, you listen, and you leave before you become tiring. The custom, I realized, tells the visitor exactly what to do, so that nobody has to invent comfort on the spot.

So on the fourth evening I went, with a loaf of bread my daughters had baked. David was sitting on a low chair near the window. I waited, as I had been told. After a moment he asked who I was, and when I said that his mother had been the midwife at both my daughters' births, his face changed. He told me that she had kept a notebook of every birth she attended, more than 2000 names, and that our street filled three pages.

"In court," he said, "a barrister always has the right words ready. This week I have had none, and it turns out that people coming to sit with us matters more than any words." We talked about his mother for twenty minutes. Then I left.

My hesitation, I now think, had been chiefly about myself. When grief comes to someone nearby, most of us should show up briefly, say little and trust the old customs to hold the rest. Mrs. Levin spent forty years arriving at strangers' houses at the hardest hour. The least we could do was walk across the street.

Questions:
Who was Mrs. Levin?
She was the midwife of the street for forty years, and she was dearly loved.
What is shiva?
Shiva is a period of mourning after a Jewish funeral, when friends visit the family at home for seven days.
What advice did the writer's friend give?
She said to come, sit, listen, wait for the family to speak first, and leave before becoming tiring.
What did David, the barrister, say about words?
He said that a barrister always has the right words in court, but that week the visits mattered more than words.
